direct_claims: This chart reports the share of young people in each surveyed country who answered "yes" to six statements about climate change in 2021.
The domain is climate attitudes and youth perceptions of climate-related threat.
The surveyed population was 1,000 young people aged 16 to 25 in each country.
The included geographies are an all-countries aggregate plus Australia, Brazil, Finland, France, India, Nigeria, the Philippines, Portugal, the United Kingdom, and the United States.
The chart comes from Our World in Data's grapher page linked in the source metadata.

In the all-countries results, emotional and institutional concern are more common than reproductive hesitation: 75% say the future is frightening and 83% say people have failed to take care of the planet, compared with 39% saying they are hesitant to have children.
Because each country surveyed 1,000 people aged 16 to 25, the chart is useful for comparing youth sentiment across countries, but it should not be treated as the views of all age groups.

In the all-countries aggregate, three statements receive majority agreement above 50% by a wide margin: humanity is doomed at 56%, future is frightening at 75%, and people have failed to take care of the planet at 83%; family security is also just above half at 52%, while hesitant to have children remains below half at 39%.
The data are from 2021, so they provide a snapshot rather than a trend over time.
derived_claims: Across all countries, the most widely endorsed statement is that people have failed to take care of the planet at 83%, while the least widely endorsed is being hesitant to have children at 39%. — derived by comparing all-country percentages across the six statements.

Several statements capture different dimensions of climate concern: existential fear such as "Humanity is doomed," household vulnerability such as "Family security is threatened," economic outlook such as "Less opportunity than their parents," reproductive hesitation, emotional outlook through "Future is frightening," and institutional or collective failure through "People have failed to take care of the planet." — derived by interpreting categories from the wording of the six survey statements.

Country differences are substantial for some statements; for example, "Future is frightening" ranges from 56% in Finland to 92% in the Philippines, a 36-point spread. — derived by computing max-min for the 'Future is frightening' column.
"Family security is threatened" ranges from 30% in Finland to 77% in the Philippines, a 47-point spread. — derived by computing max-min for the 'Family security is threatened' column.

The Philippines records the highest value among listed countries on four of the six statements: family security threatened, less opportunity than parents, future is frightening, and people have failed to take care of the planet. — derived by identifying column maxima by country.
India is highest on "Humanity is doomed" at 74%, while Brazil is highest on "Hesitant to have children" at 48%. — derived by identifying maxima for those two columns.
Finland is the lowest country on five statements, while Nigeria is lowest on "Hesitant to have children" at 23%. — derived by identifying column minima by country.

These results matter because they indicate that many young respondents see climate change not only as an environmental issue but also as a threat to their future, security, and life choices. — derived by synthesizing meaning from the six statement categories and their percentages.

The strongest all-country responses cluster around fear and perceived societal failure, suggesting that climate change is experienced by many young people as a crisis of trust and outlook as well as a policy problem. — derived by comparing all-country values for 'Future is frightening' and 'People have failed to take care of the planet' against the other statements.

Countries with especially high agreement across multiple statements, such as the Philippines, Brazil, India, and Portugal, may reflect contexts where climate risks feel more immediate or visible to young people. — derived by identifying countries with consistently high percentages across multiple columns.
The all-countries aggregate sits below the highest-scoring country on every statement shown. — derived by comparing the all-countries row with each column maximum.
The statement about people failing to take care of the planet is the only one where every listed country is at or above 75%. — derived by checking all values in that column.
